title: UK prosecutors charge two over suspected Iranian spying near RAF Fairford
description: British prosecutors on Tuesday charged two men under national security legislation over suspected Iranian intelligence activity near RAF Fairford, an airbase in southwest England. The base has been used by U.S. bombers in strikes on Iran. Mohammed Abdul Karim, 24, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police believe was Iran. Nouman Essghir, also 24, was charged with entering a prohibited location for a purpose harmful to British national security. Both men were scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday. The investigation began after five men were arrested near the base on Sept. 27 following reports of suspicious vehicles. U.S. bombers were subsequently withdrawn from RAF Fairford over security concerns, according to Reuters .

title: Pittsburgh marks eight years since Tree of Life synagogue shooting
description: Pittsburgh, Pa. will hold a public ceremony on Tuesday to commemorate the Oct. 27, 2018 mass shooting a the city's Tree of Life*Or L’Simcha Congregation. On Sunday, volunteers took part in various charitable activities, including serving meals and cleaning up Jewish cemeteries, WPXI-TV News Pittsburgh reported. The activities were carried out through the 10.27 Healing Partnership, a group that supports those impacted by the synagogue shooting, and the Friendship Circle of Pittsburgh, whose mission is to build a more inclusive community. “So many of the kids here come because this is just what we do now, and it’s been eight years, so a lot of these young kids that are here commemorating with us are really just commemorating values they’ve grown up with,” said Rivkee Rudolph, the Friendship Circle's director and co-founder. description: A former insurance executive in Ireland’s branch of the AIG firm who said his social media account had been hacked and used to vilify Jews is no longer with the company, his former boss recently told local Jews last week. AIG Ireland’s president and chief executive, Eric Andersen, informed the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland (JRCI) in an email of his firm’s parting of ways with John Gillick, former head of consumer marketing and sponsorship, The Irish Times reported on Sunday. Under Gillick’s account on X, text appeared last month that described Israel and Jews as “human scum” and Jews as “filthy dogs,” according to the report. One post stated: “Jews in Ireland need to be thrown out. They are traitors and land thieves. Our children need to be educated more about how evil Israel and Jews are,” and, “no one should associate with murdering jew war criminals.” On Sept. 2, a post on the account read: “I want to let people know that my account has been compromised by unauthorised person(s) and that recent posts containing anti-Semitic content were not written, published or endorsed by me,” and, “I unequivocally condemn the views expressed in those posts. They do not reflect my beliefs or values. I strongly oppose discrimination and hate in all forms.” Initially, AIG Ireland said the social media posts in question were “fraudulently published following the unauthorised compromise of an employee’s personal social media account.” However, in informing JCRI of Gillick’s departure, Andersen wrote that matter of the posts was the subject of an ongoing police investigation, and an internal one at AIG Ireland. JRCI Chair Orli Degani told The Irish Times that she did not know the circumstances surrounding Gillick’s departure, but welcomed AIG’s investigation, the newspaper reported.

title: Jewish Choral Conducting Institute graduates first cohort of fellows
description: The Jewish Choral Conducting Institute (JCCI), a program dedicated to high-level training of conductors of Jewish choral music, has graduated its first cohort of fellows. JCCI was created by Maestro Matthew Lazar, founder and director of the Zamir Choral Foundation, to provide professional education and pass on the tradition and experience of Jewish choral music to the next generation. The fully funded institute is made possible by a major gift from Cantor Robert Lieberman and Rabbi Vicki Lieberman. Each JCCI cohort is composed of 11-15 conducting students from around the world. During the immersive two-year program, fellows attend intensive in-person retreats, workshops and monthly online meetings and receive one-on-one mentoring sessions with Lazar and guest presenters. Lazar brings knowledge of Jewish and Western music and a deep understanding of the relationship between text and music that defines choral music. He models, encourages and nurtures the talents of a new generation of conductors of Jewish music. "The conductor integrates music, text and cultural identity with mastery and precision, creating inspiring and transformative musical moments," Lazar said. "The institute provides the specialized skills and knowledge needed to make all this possible." The inaugural group of fellows has completed the program. They were presented with a certificate in Jewish Choral Conducting and performed in a recital at the North American Jewish Choral Festival. The graduates are Shani Chamovitz, Abram Foster, Joshua Gonzalez, Matthew Gonzalez, Joel Herman, Dor Kaminka, Juliana Rappaport, Elliot Roman, Yoel Rubinstein, Nitzan Shohaam and Hadas Sturman. A new cohort of JCCI fellows recently began the program, continuing the mission to share the legacy of Jewish choral music with the next generation. "We are guided by a vision of vibrant Jewish identity through the study and performance of Jewish music at the highest level of excellence. Our goal is to create a pipeline of talented and knowledgeable conductors of Jewish choral music who will ensure the future of this rich and empowering art form," Lazar said. For more information, visit: www.zamirchoralfoundation.org .

title: Italy arrests Hamas advocate over street riots
description: Authorities in Italy last week arrested a 30-year-old academic who justified Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, massacres for allegedly organizing violent demonstrations in Milan inspired by riots in France. Youssef Siher is suspected of inciting violence for terrorist purposes, Corriere della Sera reported on Saturday. A dual citizen of Italy and Morocco, Siher was the administrator of the Instagram page “Movimento 17 Ottobre” ("October 17 Movement"), which called for demonstrations across Italy. Siher, an organizer of Palestinian anti-Israel actions of Italy, in a 2024 essay defended the Hamas-led terrorist attacks in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the report said. He wrote in the magazine Miccia : "Few in the West were able to conceive without ifs and buts of ‘Operation Al-Aqsa Flood’ for what it was: a revolutionary act of decolonization.” "Operation Al-Aqsa Flood" is the name that Hamas gave its rampage, in which terrorists killed some 1,200 people and abducted 251 others, amid other war crimes.   Siher had no criminal record before his arrest, the report said. His wife is under investigation on suspicion of the same offenses attributed to him. The Milan clashes are part of the apparent spread of rioting that began in France several weeks ago. Italian authorities have detained more than 370 people over the weekend and arrested nine in connection with the riots, in which far-left agitators have taken to the streets along with other protesters, many of African and Middle Eastern descent, to protest a diverse range of issues, from underfunding of education to racism in society. Similar protests have begun to occur in Spain, where authorities in Barcelona detained more than 100 people over the weekend.

The bishop of Blackburn, Philip North, was among the prominent officials who condemned the incident, which police are investigating as a hate crime, the report said. title: Netanyahu denies report Trump blocked Iran strike
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday denied a Financial Times report that the Jewish state recently planned to attack Iran but was stopped by U.S. President Donald Trump. "This report is not true," Netanyahu said in an interview with Israel National News . The premier declined to elaborate further. The British newspaper on Wednesday cited three sources familiar with the plans as saying that the Israel Defense Forces had prepared for a days-long campaign of intensive strikes on Iranian targets during the weekend of Oct. 10. The planned operation reportedly included attacks on nuclear facilities, power plants and other infrastructure. According to the newspaper, the offensive did not go ahead because Trump opposed resuming hostilities before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. One source said Israel and the United States could still resume military operations in the coming weeks. In the INN interview, Netanyahu said he had instructed the IDF and the Mossad to bring down the Iranian regime. He said Iran and its "axis of evil" were "weaker than ever." He warned that Tehran is still working to obtain nuclear weapons despite the damage done to its nuclear sites.

description: U.K. Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said on Wednesday that he hoped a new report detailing the rise of antisemitism in English educational institutions would "prove to be a significant step towards protecting Jewish pupils." The report, overseen by Sir David Bell, a former schools inspector, was released on Wednesday. It offers 27 recommendations to combat the phenomenon. "Antisemitism is the ultimate othering, often driven by ignorance, which is the enemy of the cohesive and empathetic society we wish to build for all citizens," Mirvis posted to X. "With this in mind, the Bell Review reveals a deeply troubling level of antisemitism in our schools and colleges and is a painful indication of how far the situation has deteriorated. I commend Sir David Bell for his important work," he said. "I also welcome the government’s decision to adopt all 27 of its recommendations and look forward to seeing them implemented in full."

title: Is Jewish unity in a polarized nation possible?
description: At a time when most Americans have lost the ability to listen to people with opposing views on political issues, how can a fractious Jewish community that is also split on denominational lines pull together? That’s the question posed by JNS editor-in-chief Jonathan Tobin. He believes that Jewish disunity has been exacerbated by the capture of the political left, which is still supported by the majority of Jews, by anti-Israel and antisemitic “progressives.” This puts even more pressure on Jewish liberals to conform to fashionable opinion on the left that poses a threat to their community’s interests and safety. He’s joined in this week’s episode of “Think Twice” by DePaul University Law professor Roberta Kwall, author of the new book , Polarized: Why American Jews Are Divided And What to Do About It . She believes that a vital Jewish center can be reconstituted if people realize that what unites them is still greater than those who seek to tear them apart. Part of the problem is that Israel, which was once thought to be a unifying factor, is now the greatest source of division, with many unaffiliated or liberal Jews no longer supportive of it, and a small but well-publicized minority actively opposed to Zionism. At the core of her effort is a statement of largely anodyne principles that she believes the overwhelming majority of Jews agree on. Among them is support for the right of Israel to exist as a Jewish and democratic state, as well as the legitimacy of criticizing its government. But for Kwall, equally important is the need to re-emphasize education and the importance of tradition to reinforce Jewish identity. In such a context, it will be easier for Jews who disagree on politics or aspects of Israeli policy to listen to each other and find common ground. title: Israeli engineering team makes history at Europe’s 24-hour solar car race
description: A team of engineering students from Afeka Academic College of Engineering in Tel Aviv made history this month, becoming the first Israeli team to compete in the iLumen European Solar Challenge in Belgium, a 24-hour solar-powered endurance race. Competing as AFEKA Racing, the students completed 197 laps—nearly 800 kilometers (490 miles)—in a solar-powered vehicle they designed and built themselves, finishing 14th overall and ranking first among the six teams competing in the challenge for the first time. The race marked the culmination of an ambitious multidisciplinary project bringing together Afeka students from mechanical, electrical, software and industrial engineering. Working across disciplines, the students combined their expertise to design and build a functioning solar race car capable of competing on the international stage. Completing a 24-hour solar endurance race tested not only the vehicle’s design and performance but also the students’ ability to solve engineering problems in real time under demanding race conditions. Over the course of the competition, the team confronted technical challenges including communication issues with the vehicle’s computer system and higher-than-expected tire wear, even performing a wheel alignment during the race to keep the car moving. “What made me most proud was seeing how the team grew throughout the project,” said Dr. Dan Herman, who leads Afeka’s Auto Club. “At the beginning, I was deeply involved in managing the project and making decisions. Over time, the students took ownership, managed themselves and learned to make those decisions together. Even when we faced challenges during the race, they worked as a team, solved every problem and kept the car moving.” Afeka is the only academic institution in Israel to offer an automotive specialization as part of its undergraduate mechanical engineering program. The solar car project builds on that focus by taking engineering education beyond the classroom and giving students hands-on experience designing and constructing a complex vehicle while collaborating across engineering disciplines. This approach extends across Afeka’s student engineering clubs, which give students opportunities to apply their knowledge across disciplines and take on ambitious real-world engineering challenges. The team sees its participation in Belgium as a foundation for the continued development of Afeka’s solar racing program. The project is designed to grow from one generation of Afeka engineers to the next. Current and future students will build on the knowledge developed by the team, while Auto Club alumni look forward to remaining involved, sharing their experience and contributing to the project even after graduation. “Engineering education is at its best when students have the opportunity to take what they learn in the classroom and apply it to complex, real-world challenges,” said Prof. Yossi Rosenwaks, president of Afeka Academic College of Engineering. “What these students accomplished in Belgium reflects the creativity, determination and interdisciplinary collaboration we strive to cultivate at Afeka. More importantly, it reflects the kind of engineers we seek to educate — engineers who can turn knowledge into action, take on ambitious challenges and help shape Israel’s technological future . We are incredibly proud of the way they represented Afeka and Israel on the international stage, and we look forward to seeing how they build on this achievement in the years ahead.” The team is already looking toward an even larger challenge: the Bridgestone World Solar Challenge in Australia, one of the world’s leading solar vehicle competitions. AFEKA Racing hopes to use the experience gained in Belgium as a foundation for bringing an Afeka-built solar car to the competition, which will take place in August 2027 and send teams on a roughly 3,000-kilometer journey from Darwin to Adelaide.
